title: Greg Doucette's maingaining: gimmicky buzzword or perennial truth?
summary: NH reviews Greg Doucette's maingaining, a rebranded lean bulk, and endorses it: naturals gain only so much muscle, so big surpluses add fat and big deficits burn muscle. Maintaining or a tiny surplus fits a lifelong pursuit, prevents dysmorphia-inducing swings and keeps focus on training; he credits Doucette as a decent gatekeeper for beginners.
claims: Maingaining is just lean bulking rebranded, made popular by Doucette's reach
He recommends naturals either maintain or run very slow, small cuts and bulks rather than massive cycles
Bulk in winter, cut in summer came from enhanced pro bodybuilders and does not work for naturals
A bigger surplus does not build more muscle for a natural, only more fat; a big deficit burns muscle as well as fat
An average trainee who is neither very overweight nor very skinny can start maingaining from day one with a tiny surplus or maintenance
A small surplus can help psychologically because the scale moves; those unhappy with their body fat can simply maintain and recomp, though progress is slower
Cycling long bulks and cuts keeps teaching the body contradictory lessons and reflects impatience for immediate visible change
Maingaining frees you from diet preoccupation so changes come from slow lean mass and performance gains
People who say maingaining does not work lack passion; it suits those who see training as a lifelong pursuit of 15 years
Skinny people still gain weight on a slow bulk; extremist heavy-bulk advocates promote body dysmorphia
Big fat-heavy bulk gains followed by losing them on a cut messes with your head and feeds dysmorphia; steady trackable maingaining soothes that anxiety
Constantly swinging calorie intake disrupts training and causes plateaus; stable intake lets you focus on training
Doucette is often wrong (far more than 2% of the time) but is a useful gatekeeper for beginners: progressive overload, flexible dieting and maingaining
